name: Name
body: Battle Forge is a monthly series that presents a new WARMACHINE scenario in each installment. Battle Forge scenarios emphasize the narrative unfolding over the course of a game and may be asymmetrical, uneven, and even somewhat experimental because the goal of Battle Forge is to create a sandbox toolset that allows for creative scenario generation and new, story-worthy experiences with WARMACHINE! Players are encouraged to modify Battle Forge scenarios in any way that makes the scenario more appropriate for their army collections and their available terrain resources. Most important of all, have fun! And if you find a better way to do something with a scenario that results in a better experience for you, let us know at feedback@privateerpress.com, so we can try it, too!

name: Name
body: Following are the key terms that will be repeated in many Battle Forge scenarios:

name: Name
body: Many scenarios utilize objectives. An objective can either be a terrain piece, a marker, or a zone designated on a terrain piece or on the map.

name: Name
body: Objective Markers are impassable terrain features and should be represented on the table with markers that are at least 20 mm in diameter. Unless otherwise specified, all Objective Markers used in a scenario should be the same size.

name: Name
body: To have more models in an area than your opponent does.

name: Name
body: An area or objective is contested if both players have models in the area or in scoring proximity to the objective at a time when scoring would take place. An area or objective is uncontested if only one player has models in the area or in scoring proximity to the objective when scoring would take place.

name: Name
body: The zone or the area of a terrain feature is held when a player occupies the area with two or more models, uncontested.

name: Name
body: An objective terrain piece or marker is secured when a player has two or more models within 1" of the objective, uncontested.

name: Name
body: Battle Forge victories can be determined by either achieving the goals of the scenario or through Victory Points, scored in a variety of ways throughout playing a scenario. Turn limits on scenarios put pressure on players to succeed within a set amount of turns, and Victory Points provide the means to determine victory when neither player has completed the primary objective of a scenario.

name: Name
body: In addition to its standard rules, each Battle Forge scenario has two random tables that add additional Victory Point-scoring opportunities for players that vary each time the scenario is played. Mission Modifiers add additional scoring opportunities based on the position of a player’s models on the table. Achievements add additional scoring opportunities based on a player’s actions taken on the battlefield. Players should roll a d6 to randomly determine Mission Modifiers and Achievements before the beginning of a game, or players can choose them at will if all players agree. It is recommended that only one Mission Modifier and one Achievement should be in effect during any match (unless you really want to get crazy).

name: Name
body: If a player makes an attack that destroys one or more friendly models, that player’s opponent gains 1 Victory Point. If a player makes an attack and destroys their own Leader model, that player immediately loses the match.

name: Name
body: In addition to objectives, Battle Forge scenarios will routinely draw on the following terrain elements. Dimensions provided are approximations, and you should feel free to substitute any terrain pieces you have available as necessary. Use the resources you have available to get close enough to maintain the spirit and intention of the scenario.

name: Name
body: An obstacle with an approximate footprint of 3/4" x 4". Barriers provide cover.

name: Name
body: Obstructions with an approximate footprint of 5" x 5".

name: Name
body: Forest areas with an approximate footprint of 5" in diameter.

name: Name
body: An obstacle with an approximate footprint of 2" x 2". Small obstacles provide cover.

name: Name
body: An elevated platform at least 1" above the table, such as a hill or terrace. Plateaus can possess multiple areas at different heights that models can be placed on, but the areas must be level to prevent models from falling over. If a model cannot be placed on a level area without risk of falling off, it cannot occupy that area. Models cannot be placed on slopes, and we recommend that plateau terrain with sloped surfaces not be used. Hill, Small—A plateau platform with a footprint approximately 6" in diameter and a level surface(s) at least 1" above the table that is large enough for five 30 mm models to be placed on. Hill, Large—A plateau with a footprint approximately 6" to 12" in diameter and a level surface(s) at least 1" above the table that is large enough for five 40 mm models to be placed on.

name: Name
body: An area of shallow water approximately 6" in diameter.

name: Name
body: An area of rubble approximately 6" in diameter.

name: Name
body: A 3" x 5" trench template.

name: Name
body: Winter has come to the Iron Kingdoms. Ammo is in short supply and won’t be replenished until the thaw. Generals need to be creative to stretch their resources while still pressing the attack against the enemy. It’s time to get up to snow good!

name: Name
body:
"SNOWBALL FIGHT"
"Snowball Fight" is designed to be played with 50-, 75-, or 100-point forces.

name: Name
body: "Snowball Fight" ends after six rounds.

name: Name
body: Players attempt to destroy each other’s bases by toppling them with massive, runaway snowballs. In order to do so, they’ll have to protect the snowballs as they increase in size and speed each round. But watch out, because snowballs are just as deadly to models as they are to the buildings they’re being launched at!

name: Name
body: Destroy your opponent’s base using a runaway snowball before they destroy your base.

name: Name
body:
The map shown below uses 2 buildings, 4 forests, 5 small hills, 3 snowball objective markers, and 2 obstacles. To represent the snowballs in the match, you’ll also need up to 5 each of 30 mm, 40 mm, 50 mm, 80 mm, and 120 mm bases, or you can cut circles of the corresponding sizes out of cardstock. You’re also going to need scratch paper or tokens to track damage on snowballs.
If you really want to take this scenario to the next level, visit a craft store and grab some foam spheres to mount on the bases!

name: Name
body:
When the match starts, each player has a 30 mm snowball in play, aimed directly at their opponent’s base.
There are three other snowball objectives on the battlefield that, when secured, are replaced by a 30 mm snowball aimed at the base of the securing player’s opponent.
During each player’s Maintenance Phase, every snowball in play moves according to the following movement rules:
- Snowballs are considered to be models that are friendly to the player who put them in play and can be targeted normally.
- Snowballs must move their full movement distance directly toward their assigned target. Snowballs move their full distance even if they contact other models. If a snowball ends its movement overlapping the base of another model, move the other model using the Rule of Least Disturbance.
- Snowballs cannot change direction or be stopped.
- Any model with the same base size or smaller that contacts or is contacted by a snowball is removed from play.
- Any Defense a snowball collides with is removed from play.

name: Name
body:
- At the end of each of the second player’s turns, all snowballs in play grow to the next size up. (30 mm snowballs become 40 mm; 40 mm snowballs become 50 mm; etc.)
- Snowballs move at different speeds, depending on their size:
- 30 mm snowballs move 2" each turn
- 40 mm snowballs move 3" each turn
- 50 mm snowballs move 4" each turn
- 80 mm snowballs move 5" each turn
- 120 mm snowballs move 6" each turn
- If a snowball collides with another snowball, the smaller snowball is removed from play and the larger snowball is replaced with a snowball the next size up. If the snowballs are the same size, randomly determine which one is removed from play and replace the remaining snowball with the next size up.
- Snowballs are DEF 10, ARM 20. If a snowball suffers a number of damage points equal to its base size in mm in a single turn, replace the snowball with a snowball of the next size down, unless it is a 30 mm snowball, in which case it is removed from play. (For instance, if a 40 mm snowball sustains 40 points of damage in a single turn, replace it with a 30 mm snowball.)

name: Name
body:
- Bases have 120 health points. When a base is impacted by a snowball, remove damage equal to the base size in mm of the snowball, then remove the snowball from play. Bases cannot be damaged in any other way. When a base is reduced to zero damage boxes, it is destroyed.
A player gains 1 Victory Point each time they launch a snowball from one of the three snowball objective markers.

name: Name
body: Roll once on both the Mission Modifiers and Achievement tables.

name: Name
body: Roll a d3 to determine the Mission Modifier for this match: 1. Blizzard—A snowstorm rages across the battlefield, giving all models Stealth. Additionally, models suffer –2 to their ranged attack rolls. 2. Katamari—On any player’s turn, any snowball that removes an opponent’s model from play is replaced with the next size up at the end of its movement. 3. Faster Frosty—Increase the distance snowballs are moved by 1".

name: Name
body: Roll a d3 to determine the Achievement for this match. 1. Happy Birthday!—The first player to launch a snowball from a snowball objective marker gains 1 additional Victory Point. 2. Snowed Under —On any turn in which one of your opponent’s models is destroyed by a snowball, gain 1 Victory Point. 3. Snow Fair!—On any turn a player reduces the size of a snowball by causing damage to it, they gain 1 Victory Point.

name: Name
body: Victory conditions are checked in the following order: Decisive Win: At the end of any of the second player’s turns, if a player’s base has been destroyed while their opponent still has a base, then their opponent wins the match. Point Advantage Win: At the end of any of the second player’s turns, if a player has 4 Victory Points or more than their opponent, that player wins the match. Last Leader Win: At the end of any of the second player’s turns, a player with the last Leader model in play wins the match. Victory Point Win: If neither player has a Leader in play at the end of any of the second player’s turns, the player with the most Victory Points wins the match.
